There's always the possibility, and many kinds of things we could make, but online communities tend not to be as good at this as once hoped because anonymity makes trust-building, coherence, and proof-of-work difficult. And, as a subculture, the Voat community seems to me to be more politically than practically focused. Not to be snarky, but this isn't exactly a community that seems that interested in doing things. Right now, who in the Voat community would you trust to collect, hold, and spend actual money/resources on behalf of everyone else? Could an escrow service for Bitcoin offer a solution? What other forms of contribution could be collectivized?

People are less uptight and more generous with sharing resources other than money. But these sorts of resources aren't as fungible for different things and are more difficult to collectivize. Some years ago there was an interesting project developed by some Swiss engineering students that had a novel strategy for crowdsourcing. They had devised a new kind of wooden space frame for housing construction that could be made from random sticks of wood and recycled cans. They designed a pair of simple table-top machines, one a kind of metal die cutter and press that would make node plates from cans and the other a kind of oversized pencil sharpener that would turn any piece of relatively straight scrap wood into a standard sized strut. And with these parts you could build a full scale home using the space frame as a space-filling structure you would finish with conventional wall panel, roofing, and flooring. The idea was that they would make and sell these simple machines to people who wanted to be in their aid network and whenever there was a call for housing aid or a disaster that needed emergency shelter all the members of the network could go collect cans and scrap wood from their homes and neighborhoods and turn them into these standard parts to send to the location needing them for construction.

The only problem was that, to make this work with common scrap materials and common postal shipping, the components of the space frame had to be rather small. So it took millions of parts to build a single house, making it rather time-consuming. But it was still an interesting approach to using crowdsourcing to turn common trash into a useful resource. Corporations have come up with other similar notions. Heineken is famous for having once developed a square glass beer bottle that was designed to be repurposed as a building block for low-cost houses. The idea was that places in need of housing could form campaigns to get beer drinkers to collect and send in their empties to help build homes.

I had once worked on a similar concept based on the Matrix building system devised by designer Ken Isaacs. I realized that there is this huge industrial capacity in the power tools that suburban people collect yet rarely make much use of. So if one could devise disaster relief shelter based on a set of modest-sized standardized modular components people could make with common materials and little skill, one might be able to crowdsource relief shelter kit production in response to disasters. But for this to work, given component sizes larger than could be shipped by mail, one needed a logistics network to gather the components into kits for bulk transport. So I turned to the churches to see if there was any interest in this. Sadly, clergy find it much easier to simply pray to god to solve problems then get off their own asses.

Recently a maker named Dave Hakkens, inventor of the Phonebloks concept, devised a set of small scale open source machines for plastic trash recycling and started a project called Precious Plastic to promote the local production of these machines and programs to locally collect and reuse plastic waste. There are an endless variety of things that can be made from recycled plastic but the most practical would be basic materials like panels and blocks or some kind of modular components, like the pontoon cubes that have been made popular in Asia. Imagine crowdsourcing your own island... Large water tanks are commonly rotomolded from recycled HDPE, sometimes including an integral foamed layer for insulaltion, and these have actually been repurposed to make antarctic research shelters. This has led to their experimentation for relief housing.

Recently, I've been studying the concept of crowdsourcing an open source space program based on hobby robotics through the creation of a Internet-managed prototype telebase; a tele-operated space outpost. Telerobotics is how we're ultimately going to have to do things in space and recently the ESA started promoting their vision of a Moonbase built by small telerobots. Though jumping the 3D printing bandwagon, this method is actually based on a very old and simple building technique once used by German military engineers in WWII to build bunkers and underground hangars called mound-formed shell construction. This has long been proposed in many variations for Moonbase construction and it well suits simple telerobots as it doesn't require much precision. Right now there's a growing hobby for RC construction machines featuring alloy construction and quite powerful mini-hydraulic systems. These machines can be just as large as the robots ESA proposes to use and are capable of some serious earth-moving work. Repurposing components from these models along with other off-the-shelf components it's not perfectly feasible to create analog space telerobots that can be controlled over the Internet. So I've been proposing the idea of creating a mock-up lunar telebase as a new Internet-based alternative to the old community model train layout, using these home-brew robots to construction a full-scale mockup of the proposed ESA Moonbase. This could be a lot of fun while actually performing some serious space telerobot R&D. These models are a bit expensive though (some fancier ones exceed $10,000) but Chinese companies are coming into the hobby, keeping them within the price range of a desktop PC. Getting commercial sponsorship, perhaps from actual construction machine companies, could help get this going faster.
